demo_input.text: banana apple orange fruit tropical sweet

step_explanations.title: Validate Input Text
step_explanations.description: Check that input has sufficient words to learn subword patterns.
step_explanations.why_it_matters: Need enough words to learn meaningful subword representations. More data = better OOV handling.

step_explanations.title: Extract Character N-grams
step_explanations.description: For each word, extract all character n-grams (typically 3-6 chars) and add word boundaries (<, >).
step_explanations.why_it_matters: Subword n-grams capture morphological information (prefixes, suffixes, roots) that help with OOV and rare words.

step_explanations.title: Train with Skip-gram + Negative Sampling
step_explanations.description: Learn embeddings for each n-gram and whole word, optimizing the Skip-gram objective with negative sampling.
step_explanations.why_it_matters: This is the core learning - the model discovers that subwords carry meaning (e.g., '-ing' = verb, '-tion' = noun).

step_explanations.title: Compute Similarities & Handle OOV
step_explanations.description: Measure cosine similarity between word vectors. Demonstrate OOV handling by computing embedding for an unseen word using its n-grams.
step_explanations.why_it_matters: OOV handling is FastText's key advantage over Word2Vec - it can embed any word, even never seen during training.

formula_cards.title: FastText Word Representation
formula_cards.formula: v_w = sum of (subword_n-gram embeddings for w) + whole_word_embedding
formula_cards.explanation: Each word is represented by summing embeddings of all its character n-grams (typically 3-6 chars) plus the whole-word embedding.

formula_cards.title: FastText Skip-gram Objective
formula_cards.formula: J(θ) = Σ log P(w_O|w_I) = Σ log σ(v_{w_O}·v_{w_I}) + Σ log σ(-v_{neg}·v_{w_I})
formula_cards.explanation: Same as Word2Vec Skip-gram with negative sampling, but v_w now includes subword information.

formula_cards.title: OOV Handling
formula_cards.explanation: Out-of-vocabulary words get embeddings from their character n-grams, even if not seen during training.
formula_cards.example: 'bananarama' → n-grams include 'banana' overlap with known word 'banana' → meaningful embedding!

hover_annotations.definition: Substrings of length n (typically 3-6) extracted from words with boundary symbols (<, >).
hover_annotations.formula_meaning: For 'banana' with n=3: <ba, ban, ana, nan, ana, na> (note: < and > are boundaries)
hover_annotations.common_mistake: Forgetting word boundaries (<, >) which help distinguish prefixes/suffixes from middle n-grams

hover_annotations.definition: Words not seen during training. FastText can embed them using character n-grams; Word2Vec cannot.
hover_annotations.formula_meaning: v_oov = Σ embeddings(n-grams in oov) - composes embedding from known subword parts
hover_annotations.example: 'bananarama' → n-grams overlap with 'banana' → gets meaningful embedding despite never being trained
hover_annotations.common_mistake: Thinking FastText eliminates OOV entirely (it reduces the problem but very rare n-grams may still be unknown)

references.title: Enriching Word Vectors with Subword Information
references.authors: Bojanowski, P., Grave, E., Joulin, A., and Mikolov, T.
references.relevance: FastText paper introducing character n-gram embeddings to handle OOV and improve morphologically rich languages.

references.title: Bag of Tricks for Efficient Text Classification
references.authors: Joulin, A., Grave, E., Bojanowski, P., and Mikolov, T.
references.relevance: FastText for text classification - shows how subword info improves performance on rare words and morphologically rich languages.

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: FastText looks at pieces of words (like 'ban', 'ana') to understand meaning. This helps it understand new words it hasn't seen before!
receiver_mode_explanations.teaching_notes: Show OOV word prediction. Compare with Word2Vec which can't handle OOV.

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: FastText = Word2Vec + subword info. Each word = sum of character n-gram (3-6) embeddings + whole-word embedding. Handles OOV via n-grams.
receiver_mode_explanations.technical_detail: N-gram range: minn=3, maxn=6 typical. Skip-gram with negative sampling. For OOV 'bananarama', sum embeddings of '<ba', 'ban', ..., 'rama', 'ma>' (if seen during training).

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: FastText's subword approach is especially beneficial for morphologically rich languages (Turkish, Finnish, Arabic) and rare words. Research shows 10-20% improvement on rare words vs. Word2Vec. Limitations: more parameters, slower training. Led to subword-based models like BPE in BERT/GPT.
receiver_mode_explanations.technical_detail: Limitations: more memory (need n-gram embeddings), slower training. Comparison: BPE (used in BERT/GPT) is another subword approach but merges frequent pairs instead of using character n-grams.

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: FastText trains slower than Word2Vec (more parameters for n-grams). Use gensim or Facebook's original implementation. OOV is automatic - just pass any word.
receiver_mode_explanations.technical_detail: Complexity: O(N×w×(V+Ngrams)×d). Memory: O((V+Ngrams)×d). API: gensim.models.FastText, or load pre-trained: fasttext.util.load_model('cc.en.300.bin').

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: FastText introduces subword linguistics to embeddings. Show how morphology (prefixes, suffixes) helps with rare and OOV words.
receiver_mode_explanations.teaching_notes: Quiz: How does FastText handle OOV? Exercise: Manually compute n-grams for 'running'. Compare Word2Vec vs. FastText on rare words.

research_context: FastText (Bojanowski et al., 2017) addressed Word2Vec's OOV limitation by incorporating character n-gram information. It's particularly effective for morphologically rich languages and rare words. The subword idea influenced modern tokenization in BERT (WordPiece) and GPT (BPE).

teaching_notes.summary: FastText extends Word2Vec with character n-gram embeddings, enabling out-of-vocabulary word handling and better rare word representations.
quiz_questions: How does FastText represent a word using subwords?
Why can FastText handle OOV words while Word2Vec cannot?
What are the typical n-gram sizes used in FastText, and why?
classroom_demo_tips: Visualize subword n-grams for a morphologically complex word
Compare OOV handling: FastText succeeds, Word2Vec fails
Show similarity improvements on rare words vs. Word2Vec
common_misconceptions: FastText eliminates OOV entirely (false - very rare n-grams may still be unknown)
FastText is always better than Word2Vec (false - for common words, they're similar; FastText is slower to train)
